attacks.claim: The cost math treats a daily token volume as monthly. 38M lines/day x 60 tokens = 2.28B tokens/day, which at $0.50/M is about $1,140/day, or roughly $34k/month. That is about 23x the $1,500/month approved budget, so the 'within budget' conclusion is false.
attacks.evidence: "Input: 38M lines x 60 tokens = 2.28B tokens -> ~$1,140" and "Estimated total: ~$1,150/month, within the $1,500 budget." (the 38M figure is stated as lines/day)

attacks.claim: No spend cap, sampling, per-service token budget, or cost alarm is defined. Peak days (61M lines) and incident-time log surges push the already over-budget spend higher, with nothing to bound it.
attacks.evidence: "peak day 61M" and ABSENT: any token budget, rate limit, sampling, or cost alert

attacks.claim: Every log line in each 5-minute window goes to the LLM with no truncation or sampling. Average volume is already about 4,400 lines (~264k tokens) per service-window, and chatty services or incidents will be far larger. Calls are likely to exceed context limits, time out, or be very slow.
attacks.evidence: "sends the last 5 minutes of logs per service to the LLM" and ABSENT: max input size, truncation, pre-aggregation, or sampling policy

attacks.claim: The staffing plan assumes both engineers are 100% on the build, but the charter says on-call and interrupts take about 50% of their time. Real capacity is about 6 eng-weeks against a 12 eng-week estimate with no slack, so the 6-week schedule is unachievable as planned.
attacks.evidence: "on-call/interrupt work averages 50% of their time" vs "both platform engineers full-time for 6 weeks (2 x 6 = 12 eng-weeks)"

attacks.claim: log-tap subscribes to the shared Vector pipeline for all 30 services. A slow or stuck subscriber could cause backpressure or log drops that hurt existing sinks, and the plan defines no isolation or drop policy.
attacks.evidence: "subscribes to the existing Vector pipeline ... forwards every application log line" and ABSENT: backpressure handling, isolation, or drop policy

attacks.claim: The plan defines no timeouts, retries, or fallback for the LLM, queue, or PagerDuty steps, and no alerting on summarizer failure. Stale summaries can be posted into incidents with no staleness marker.
attacks.evidence: "the PagerDuty incident gets an auto-comment with the latest summaries" and ABSENT: timeouts, retries, staleness indicator, health alerts

attacks.claim: Log content is partly attacker-influenceable and feeds an LLM whose output, including the 'suspected deploy' field, is posted into incidents. The plan has no input delimiting or output validation. Impact is limited because summaries are advisory.
attacks.evidence: "suspected deploy" and ABSENT: prompt-injection mitigation or labeling summaries as untrusted

attacks.claim: Redaction covers only emails, tokens, card numbers and IPs, so names and free-text customer data can still reach the vendor. No retention period or access control is stated for the stored summaries or the PagerDuty comments. Zero-retention and a DPA partly mitigate this.
attacks.evidence: "masks emails, tokens, card numbers and IPs" and ABSENT: summary retention and access control

attacks.claim: The design depends on a single model vendor, with no stated data residency region or fallback provider.
attacks.evidence: "Model: Corvid-mini" and ABSENT: residency region, fallback provider

attacks.claim: The MTTR target rests on the unmeasured assumption that 15-20 minutes go to grepping logs. The launch gate (70% useful, 5% misleading) is not justified, and the grading protocol is thin.
attacks.evidence: "instead of spending the first 15-20 minutes grepping logs" and ABSENT: a measured triage-time baseline

attacks.claim: No kill switch or feature flag is described for the PagerDuty auto-comment path. The path is advisory and easy to turn off in practice.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: feature flag or rollback procedure
